questions.prompt: Match each failure mode to the mechanism that contains it.
questions.explanation:
Each mechanism targets one specific shape of failure.

Request coalescing collapses many identical in-flight requests into one, so a cold cache entry does not produce a stampede. A circuit breaker stops a failing dependency from consuming the caller's threads and taking it down too. Quorum writes stop two halves of a partitioned cluster both believing they are authoritative. Virtual nodes spread one hot key range across many physical nodes rather than landing it all on one.

questions.prompt: Your health check pings /health, which returns 200 whenever the process is running. A deploy leaves instances unable to reach the database, but they stay in rotation and serve errors. What is the actual defect?
options: The health check interval is too long
The health check tests liveness when routing needs readiness
The load balancer needs more aggressive retries
The instances should be terminated on any error
questions.explanation:
Liveness answers "is this process alive" — restart it if not. Readiness answers "can this instance serve a real request right now" — take it out of rotation if not. Routing decisions need the second.

A readiness check that exercises the dependencies a request actually needs would have failed here and pulled the instances out. Shortening the interval only reaches the wrong answer faster; more retries spread the errors across more instances.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a backward-compatible schema change that adds a required column, with zero downtime.
items: Deploy code that writes both old and new columns
Deploy code that reads the new column
questions.explanation:
Every step has to leave both the old and new code versions working, because during a rolling deploy both are running at once.

Adding the column nullable is safe for old code, which ignores it. Writing both keeps new rows complete while old rows are still being filled. Only once the backfill is done can reads rely on it, and only once every row has a value can the constraint be added without failing.

Getting this order wrong is one of the most common causes of self-inflicted downtime.
